lesson.title: When the Bubble Burst: The Crash of 1929
lesson.summary: After years of a soaring, debt-fueled bull market, Wall Street collapsed over a period of days in late October 1929, a dramatic and highly visible symptom of deeper weaknesses in the American economy.
lesson.body:
The consumer culture of the 1920s, with its enthusiasm for buying on credit and installment plans, extended naturally into the stock market. Ordinary Americans, not just professional investors, poured money into stocks through most of the decade, encouraged by years of rising prices and a widespread belief that prosperity would simply continue. A key feature of this boom was margin buying, which let an investor purchase stock while putting down as little as 10 percent of its price in cash and borrowing the rest from a broker. That leverage magnified gains on the way up, but it also meant that even a modest drop in prices could wipe out an investor's stake and trigger a forced sale, which pushed prices down further and triggered more forced sales in turn.

By the autumn of 1929, the market had already grown shaky. Panic selling struck on Thursday, October 24, a day remembered as Black Thursday. A brief recovery followed, but the market gave way again on Monday, October 28, and Tuesday, October 29, the two days that saw the sharpest one-day percentage losses of the crash and that are remembered as Black Monday and Black Tuesday. Across these few days, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost roughly a quarter of its value.

It is important to understand that the crash was not a single afternoon of panic but the start of a much longer decline. The market kept sliding for years afterward and did not hit bottom until 1932, by which point it had fallen close to 90 percent from its peak in September 1929. The nation's continued commitment to the gold standard, a system in which the dollar's value was tied to a fixed quantity of gold, limited how freely the Federal Reserve felt it could expand credit or cut interest rates to cushion the fall, a constraint that would matter more and more as the broader economic crisis deepened in the years that followed.

The crash devastated investors and shattered public confidence, but it is best understood as a trigger and an accelerant rather than the single cause of what came next. The deeper and more complicated question of why a stock market crash turned into a decade-long depression is the subject of the next chapter.
